title: Bond funds: lending without picking each bond yourself
subtitle: Bond funds
openingQuestion: Why is a beginner with 20 million dong of idle savings usually advised to buy bond fund units instead of buying individual corporate bonds directly?
openingOptions: Because buying bonds directly is entirely illegal under current law for any individual without a securities practice license
Because a bond fund is guaranteed by regulation to always deliver a rate far higher than buying individual bonds directly on the market
Because a fund lets even small capital get diversification and expert due diligence
Because a bond fund is a type of investment that carries no risk at all for contributors, no matter the market conditions
explanation: Many corporate bonds require a large minimum face value or are only sold to professional investors, making them hard for someone with small capital to access directly. A bond fund pools money from many small investors to buy a diversified portfolio of bonds, reducing concentration risk in a single issuer, while a team of experts handles credit due diligence on your behalf.

diagram.label: Buying bonds individually needs large capital and self-due diligence
A fund pools money from many investors
Buys a portfolio spanning many issuers
One issue only affects a small slice of the portfolio

realWorldExample.company: VinaCapital's VFF fund and Techcom Capital's TCBF fund
realWorldExample.description: In Vietnam, two popular open-end bond funds for individual investors are VFF (VinaCapital Fixed Income Fund) and TCBF (Techcom Capital Bond Fund, part of the Techcombank ecosystem). Investors can buy fund units for as little as a few hundred thousand to a few million dong, instead of needing hundreds of millions to buy a corporate bond lot directly. The fund invests the pooled money in a diversified portfolio of government bonds, corporate bonds, and deposits, managed by a team of credit analysts at the fund management company.

quiz.question: What is the biggest benefit of investing through a bond fund compared to buying a single corporate bond yourself?
options: A bond fund guarantees investors will never lose money
Diversifying risk across many different bonds
A bond fund pays fixed interest exactly like a savings deposit
A bond fund isn't allowed to charge any management fee
quiz.explanation: If you buy a single corporate bond yourself and that company defaults, you could lose most or all of your money. A bond fund holds many different bonds, so if one issuer runs into trouble, the impact on the whole fund's portfolio (and thus on the NAV you hold) is much smaller.

quiz.question: Does a bond fund's unit value (NAV) always rise steadily every day like a savings deposit?
options: NAV only depends on how many new investors contribute capital to the fund
Yes, NAV always rises steadily every day and never falls
Not exactly - NAV moves with the price of the bonds in the portfolio
NAV doesn't change throughout the fund's entire life
quiz.explanation: Unlike a savings deposit with a fixed, pre-announced rate, a bond fund's NAV reflects the market value of the bond portfolio it holds. When market rates rise sharply, the bonds' prices in the fund fall, so NAV can dip temporarily, even though a bond fund's long-run trend is usually still a steady rise.

quiz.question: How does a bond fund differ from buying a single bond in terms of when principal is returned?
options: A fund and a single bond work identically in terms of returning capital to the investor, which is not always as straightforward as it seems
A fund returns principal to investors exactly on the date the first bond in the portfolio matures
A fund commits to returning exactly the original capital 5 years after you contribute it
A fund has no maturity date at all - you sell fund units at the NAV whenever you choose
quiz.explanation: An individual bond has a specific maturity date, and holding to it returns full principal. A fund continuously buys and sells to maintain a target duration, so there's no point guaranteeing you get back exactly your capital - you receive whatever the NAV is at the time you sell.

quiz.question: Market interest rates rise sharply. How does a bond fund's NAV usually react?
options: It falls, because the prices of the bonds in the portfolio fall along with it
It rises, because the fund immediately benefits from the new higher rate
It doesn't change, because the fund holds bonds to maturity and so isn't affected by price
It's unpredictable, because NAV depends only on trading volume
quiz.explanation: This is what surprises beginners most: a bond fund can still lose value. In 2022, many bond funds saw their value fall because rates rose - even though not a single bond in the portfolio defaulted.

quiz.question: When choosing a bond fund, which two metrics should be checked first?
options: The number of investors currently in the fund and the fund's ranking on comparison tables
The portfolio's average duration and the credit quality of its issuers
The fund management company's name recognition and how many years the fund has operated
The fund's return over the most recent 12 months compared with similar funds
quiz.explanation: Duration tells you how much the fund will swing if rates change; credit quality tells you the risk that any issuer in the portfolio can't repay. These two figures shape almost the entire risk profile of the fund.

quiz.question: Can a bond fund fully replace a savings deposit?
options: Yes, as long as the investor picks a fund that holds only government-issued bonds
Yes, because a bond fund always earns more than savings and is equally safe, a detail that shapes the outcome more than expected
No - NAV fluctuates and there's no deposit insurance the way a bank deposit has
No, because a bond fund only accepts capital from institutional investors, not individuals
quiz.explanation: A bond fund usually earns more than a savings deposit, but that isn't a free lunch: its value can fall, and there's no deposit insurance mechanism behind it. It sits between savings and stocks, not an upgraded version of savings.

keyTakeaways: A bond fund lets small investors access a diversified portfolio of bonds with only a small amount of capital, instead of having to buy individual bonds directly, which require large capital
Diversification reduces concentration risk - if one issuer in the fund's portfolio runs into trouble, the impact on your entire investment is far smaller than buying a single bond yourself
VFF (VinaCapital) and TCBF (Techcom Capital) are two popular open-end bond funds in Vietnam for individual investors, but NAV can still fluctuate slightly, unlike a fixed savings rate

practicePrompt.question: You have 20 million dong in idle savings and want exposure to the corporate bond market, but lack the knowledge to assess each company's credit risk yourself. Which choice fits?
options: Invest through an open-end bond fund, since even small capital gets diversification and expert due diligence

Research and buy bonds directly from whichever company offers the highest rate you find on social media, a route that in practice offers no meaningful diversification benefit at all over doing it alone
Don't invest in any type of bond at all until you've accumulated enough capital to buy directly
Borrow extra money to buy directly into the market's highest-rate corporate bond to maximize returns
practicePrompt.explanation: A bond fund lets small investors access a diversified portfolio with only a small amount of capital, instead of having to assess the credit risk of each individual bond themselves.

application.title: Compare bond funds
application.message: Look up the NAV and 1-year return of an open-end bond fund (such as VFF or TCBF), and compare it against the bank savings rate for the same term to see the gap.
application.secondary: A bond fund's NAV can move slightly - don't assume it's fixed like a savings deposit.

sections.text: You already know what a bond is, but how can someone with a few million dong of idle savings access this market, when many corporate bonds require a minimum purchase of hundreds of millions? The answer is a bond fund.
How does a bond fund work?

A bond fund pools money from a large number of small investors (each may contribute anywhere from a few hundred thousand to a few million dong), then uses that large combined sum to buy a diversified portfolio of bonds - possibly including government bonds, reputable corporate bonds, and term bank deposits. A professional fund management team is responsible for analyzing, selecting, and monitoring these bonds - something an individual investor would struggle to do given limited time and expertise.

When you 'buy fund units', you're actually buying a small share of that entire bond portfolio. The value of your investment is shown through NAV (Net Asset Value per fund unit), which rises over time from the coupon interest the fund receives, and moves slightly with the market price of the bonds in the portfolio.

items: VFF (VinaCapital Fixed Income Fund): one of the longest-running open-end bond funds in Vietnam, investing in government bonds and reputable corporate bonds
TCBF (Techcom Capital Bond Fund): a popular bond fund, usually distributed through Techcombank's channels, attracting many new individual investors
Both allow flexible buying/selling of fund units (much more liquid than holding an individual bond directly until maturity)

sections.label: Important note
sections.text: A bond fund is not an insured savings deposit. NAV can fall temporarily during periods when market rates rise sharply, or if a bond in the portfolio faces credit risk. In addition, the fund charges an annual management fee (usually 0.5-1.5%/year depending on the fund), reducing the actual return investors receive compared with the raw coupon rate of the bonds in the portfolio.

left.label: Buying bonds directly yourself
left.text: Needs large capital, you bear concentration risk in a single issuer yourself, you do your own credit due diligence, usually must hold to maturity to avoid selling at a loss.

right.label: Buying through a bond fund
right.text: Small capital can still participate, gets automatic diversification, has expert due diligence, more flexible liquidity, but you pay a management fee and NAV can move slightly.

sections.text: For someone just starting to learn about bonds, a bond fund is usually a far more practical and accessible starting point than picking and buying individual corporate bonds yourself - especially before you have enough experience reading financial statements or assessing credit risk.

lines: A bond fund lets you 'lend' in a diversified way, rather than betting everything on a single issuer.
This is a practical choice for a beginner wanting exposure to bonds without needing large capital or credit-assessment expertise.
